directive: The new Roman-authorized expedition continues from the camp beyond the first difficult pass while established estate administration, correspondence, agricultural management, and documentary inquiry continue independently.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION'S FIELD INDEX ESTABLISHES A BROADER APENNINE FRAME
events.body: The field scribes begin the week by organizing the country beyond the first difficult pass within a broader Apennine geographic frame. Their comparison uses the direction of the ridges, the character of the valleys, the movement of water, and the routes described by people who have traveled through the region before. The entry is deliberately broader than a town or settlement because the expedition has still not established its exact position. The scribes distinguish what the expedition has personally inspected from geographic names and descriptions supplied by others. The result is a more useful working map without pretending that an uncertain location has been conclusively identified. The field index is sealed and carried with the expedition as it prepares to test the lower route observed beyond the camp.

events.title: A LOWER TRACK OFFERS A NEW LINE OF MOVEMENT BEYOND THE FIRST PASS
events.body: A local guide identifies a lower track that leaves the broken ground near the first pass and descends toward a chain of easier slopes. The route is not described as a known Roman road, and the expedition does not assume that the guide's account is correct simply because it sounds plausible. Valerius sends the party far enough along the track to test its footing and observe where its water points lie. The examination reveals a route that can be used by the expedition under careful movement, although its farther course remains uncertain. Provisions are consumed during the additional survey, and the scribes record the route as a tested possibility rather than an established destination. The finding gives the expedition another way forward without resolving where the journey will ultimately lead.

events.title: A DEPENDABLE SPRING GIVES THE EXPEDITION ROOM TO CONTINUE THE SURVEY
events.body: While following the lower track, the expedition reaches a dependable spring that is easier to use than the water point described in the earlier route account. The discovery allows the carried vessels to be replenished and removes an immediate limitation on continuing the survey. Local inhabitants confirm that the spring is known to them, but their statements remain separate from the expedition's own observation of the water source. The scribes note the spring's position relative to the track and the surrounding slopes. The finding does not identify a city or reveal the expedition's final objective, but it creates a verified supply point within the route record. The water source is therefore preserved as direct geographic evidence for future movement.

events.title: THE PURCHASED FIELDS CONTINUE THROUGH THE HEIGHT OF SPRING WORK
events.body: At the estate, the purchased tract continues through the demanding portion of its spring work while the expedition remains away from the household. Stewards coordinate labor and watering with the older acreage and keep the recently acquired ground separately marked in the property records. Grain and fodder are issued for the longer working days, creating another ordinary demand on the estate's available provisions. The established access arrangement with nearby smallholders remains in force, and no new boundary question is opened. Agriculture is already at the campaign's recorded ceiling, so the continued work does not produce a further agricultural-point increase. The household instead records the actual consequence through the consumption of available supply resources.

events.title: MARCELLUS RECEIVES THE EXPEDITION'S DOCUMENTARY METHOD
events.body: The estate's scribes prepare a response to Marcus Claudius Marcellus concerning the method used to record the expedition's geographic evidence. The response explains that firsthand observations, guide testimony, and inherited geographic descriptions are being preserved as separate classes of information. The method mirrors the documentary discipline already used in the raid dossier associated with Aulus Vettius. Marcellus's inquiry therefore becomes connected to the expedition without changing its route or imposing a destination. The correspondence establishes a common standard for comparing the field record with the earlier household evidence. The archive gains another layer of documentary continuity while the expedition itself continues independently.

events.title: A SEALED ROMAN COURIER BRINGS A REQUEST FOR PRELIMINARY EXPEDITION NOTES
events.body: A Roman courier arrives with a sealed request for a preliminary copy of the expedition's newest geographic observations. The request does not order the expedition to return and does not name a new destination for the journey. Instead, it asks that the observations already gathered be copied carefully enough for Roman readers to distinguish firsthand findings from reports supplied by guides and travelers. Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer's correspondence is kept with the packet because his established connection already forms part of the Roman documentary chain surrounding Valerius's work. The expedition scribes prepare the requested material without surrendering the originals or changing the field record. The arrival makes the expedition's work newly visible to Roman correspondents while leaving the journey itself in Valerius's hands.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION FINDS A SECONDARY PASSAGE BEYOND THE FIRST DIFFICULT PASS
events.body:
You wake before the camp has fully stirred, with the route papers from the first pass laid beside the field record.
The country ahead is still unfamiliar, but the difficult pass behind you has changed the question facing the expedition from whether a road exists to which road can actually be used.
Several lines appear to offer passage through the ridges, and from the camp it is impossible to know which one will remain practical once the animals and loads are committed.
The purpose of the expedition remains unchanged: examine the country directly and produce a record that can be carried back into Roman hands.
The wider campaign ledger records 394 soldiers, but it does not establish a separate strength for this expedition, so you do not invent a detachment number.
Instead, you judge the movement by the men, animals, loads, water, and hours of usable light actually before you.
The local guide points toward a narrow break between two shoulders of rising ground.
You leave the easier track and walk the opening yourself before allowing the column to follow.
The first section is rough, but it is not blocked, and the slope beyond it falls more gradually than the face of the earlier pass.
Then the ground turns sharply and hides what lies beyond the bend.
You move farther until the route opens again and a second passage appears beyond the first line of ridges.
For a moment the discovery looks almost trivial, because it is only another piece of ground.
But the practical value becomes clear when you see that the new passage avoids the steepest section that forced the expedition to slow during the earlier crossing.
You turn back toward the men and animals and begin organizing the movement through the new line of travel.
The loads go first where the footing is soundest, and the animals are brought through the narrowest section one at a time.
Nothing spectacular happens, and there is no enemy or great settlement waiting beyond the ridge.
Instead, the expedition succeeds at the difficult work for which it was sent: determining by direct experience that a route exists where earlier accounts had left the country ambiguous.
You stop at a sheltered point and compare the new passage against the statements already gathered before the march.
One earlier account had implied that the higher ground would force the expedition into a dead end; your own inspection shows that at least one usable lower alternative exists.
You preserve the older testimony rather than destroying it, because a useful field record must show what was believed before observation changed the picture.
The scribes begin copying the route while the details are still fresh.
They mark the turns, the difficult footing, the safer sections, and the relationship between the first pass and this newly tested passage.
You correct one description that was too confident and replace it with language that distinguishes what the party actually saw from what the guide claimed lay farther ahead.
The correction does not weaken the expedition's record; it makes the boundary between evidence and assumption clearer.
As the light falls, the route ahead remains open but still unexplored beyond the section you have personally tested.
You establish the temporary camp near the safer ground rather than forcing the party farther into country that has not yet been inspected.
That evening the route register, the water notes, and the earlier testimony lie together on the ground before you.
You can now see the expedition's progress as a chain of tested observations rather than a collection of guesses.
The first difficult pass is no longer the limit of the journey.
The secondary passage is now another verified line of movement, and it gives the expedition a practical route for the next stage without inventing a final destination.
You look into the darkness beyond the camp and know that the country is still unfinished work.
The journey has not returned you to Rome, and no final objective has been reached.
But the expedition is no longer moving blindly through an untested landscape.
It has learned how one difficult obstacle can be bypassed by careful inspection, patient movement, and evidence kept separate from rumor.
The scribes seal the day's route register.
The men settle beside the new camp, while the road beyond remains open for another day's investigation.

events.title: THE SECONDARY ROUTE REGISTER IS SEALED FOR THE NEXT STAGE
events.body: Before the next march, the expedition scribes complete a clean copy of the secondary route and place it with the account of the first difficult pass. The register separates direct observations from guide testimony and preserves the route's exact tested section without pretending that its farther course is known. A notation from Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer's correspondence remains attached to the documentary packet, continuing the established Roman connection. The field party therefore begins its next stage with two tested geographic obstacles recorded and a clearer working route through the country immediately ahead. The expedition remains active, and the final destination is still unresolved.
